title: Gill, Pant, Jadeja and Siraj honoured as India dominate prestigious Wisden award
content:
India dominate this year’s prestigious Wisden Cricketers Almanack awards with four of the five cricketers of the year coming from the side who drew 2-2 with England last summer.

Captain Shubman Gill is honoured along with his India team-mates Ravindra Jadeja, Rishabh Pant and Mohammed Siraj in an award that is based on performances in the English season. England’s Haseeb Hameed, who led Nottinghamshire to the County Championship title last year, completes the five.

The naming of the five Wisden cricketers of the year, an award that can only be won once, is one of the oldest traditions in the sport, with this year’s Almanack — published on Thursday — the 163rd edition of what is widely known as the ‘cricketing bible’.

It is the first time four Indians have featured in the same year — the previous Indian high was the naming of jasprit Bumrah and Rohit Sharma in 2022 — and the first time four cricketers from any visiting side to England have taken the awards since Australia dominated the 1973 edition of the big yellow book. In 1949, all five cricketers of the year came from the Australian ‘Invincibles’ side who dominated the 1948 English summer.

Gill, who also takes the more recent Wisden Trophy for his twin centuries in the Edgbaston Test, is recognised for his prolific and stylish contributions with the bat in an enthralling Test series, with Wisden editor Lawrence Booth writing in the Almanack: “Shubman Gill’s run-making dominated the Anderson-Tendulkar Test series, his tally of 754 the most in a series for India against England. That included a remarkable double of 269 and 161 at Edgbaston, in between hundreds at Headingley and Old Trafford.”

Jadeja is recognised for his integral role in India’s summer, topping their averages with 516 runs at an average of 86. His six scores of 50 or more included a match-saving century in Manchester.

Pant’s helter-skelter excellence was one of the summer’s highlights, not least at Headingley where he made 134 and 118. He added three half-centuries — the last after breaking his foot. Siraj took more wickets, 23, than anyone in the England-India Test series, securing a 2-2 draw with a last-ditch 5-104 at the Oval, including three of England’s final four wickets on a dramatic final morning, as the tourists won by six runs.

Hameed, meanwhile, captained Notts to their first County Championship title in 15 years and led their charge with 1,258 runs at an average of 66. He carried his bat twice and converted two of his four hundreds into doubles.

The modern Wisden is not exclusively about the English summer and the Leading Cricketers in the World awards go to Mitchell Starc for his 55 Test wickets for Australia in 2025 and Deepti Sharma, who helped India’s women to World Cup glory on home soil. She scored 215 runs and taking 22 wickets in the tournament.

The 1,520 page long book again combines the serious with the light-hearted and begins with Booth, editing his 15th Wisden, taking England to task for their miserable Ashes capitulation in his notes that still carry enormous weight in the cricketing world.

“England arrived for the Ashes hell-bent on making history and ended up being laughed out of town,” writes Booth. “Much of the misery was self-inflicted: from the paper thin preparation, via a string of schoolboy dismissals, to the revelation of Harry Brook’s scrape with a nightclub bouncer in New Zealand. England were feckless, reckless and legless.”

But the Almanack ends on a traditionally light and left-field note with the index of unusual occurrences that are included this year, including ‘butterfly stops play’, ‘captain’s haircut sparks ill-feeling’, and ‘mobile phone appears on a good length’.
